string-array.name: wellness_tip_bodies
string-array.item: Cleaning your workspace at the end of the day helps your mind rest.
Opening the curtains when you wake up lets sunlight improve your mood immediately.
Getting ready, even if you\'re staying in, helps you feel more prepared for the day.
Try eating without looking at your phone. Enjoying the flavour of food calms the senses.
Drinking a glass of water when you get up helps your body wake up gently.
Walking for ten minutes outside helps you see things more clearly.
Avoiding excess sweets prevents your emotions from spiking and dropping suddenly.
Picking up what\'s out of place before bed helps you wake up with less stress.
Stretching your arms and neck relieves tension that builds up unnoticed.
Reading something positive before bed prepares your heart for deep rest.
Saying "thank you" for something small strengthens bonds of friendship.
Listening to something soft while doing chores makes the time pass better.
Try not to multi-task. Focusing on just one thing gives more satisfaction.
Going to bed at the same time gives security to your body and mind.
Caring for a small plant brings a sense of calm and life to your environment.
Speak to yourself with affection, as you would speak to a good friend.
Turning off screens an hour before bed helps your brain relax.
Giving full attention when someone speaks makes the relationship deeper.
When finishing a task, no matter how small, recognise the effort made.
When a tense moment arrives, stop and take three deep breaths.
Smiling when you wake up — even briefly — signals your brain that today is a good day.
Splashing cold water on your face resets your alertness in seconds.
When your mind feels full, write down everything on a piece of paper. It creates instant relief.
Playing sounds of rain or birdsong while you work lowers stress without distraction.
If something takes less than two minutes, do it now. Small tasks pile up into big pressure.
A genuine hug for at least six seconds releases oxytocin and reduces tension.
Preparing a meal from scratch, even a simple one, brings you into the present moment.
If a social media account makes you feel worse, mute or unfollow it. Your feed is your environment.
Progress doesn\'t need to be big. Every step forward deserves a quiet celebration.
Asking someone for help isn\'t weakness — it\'s trust, and trust builds connection.
Even 10 minutes of movement releases endorphins that lift your mood for hours.
Exercise reduces cortisol and adrenaline — the stress hormones — while boosting serotonin and dopamine naturally.
You don\'t need a gym. Five squats, a short walk, or dancing to one song all count as movement.
A 15-minute walk every day does more for your wellbeing than one hard workout per week.

A guided walkthrough to process a difficult interaction and grow from it.
Processing conflict takes courage. You\'ve taken an important step toward growth.

string-array.name: conflict_step_questions
string-array.item: Describe the situation as factually as possible — just the facts, no interpretations.
What emotions did you feel during and after this interaction?
How do you think the other person was feeling? What might they have needed in that moment?
Honestly — what role did you play in how this unfolded? Is there anything you\'d do differently?
What is one concrete action you could take to improve this situation or relationship?

string-array.name: conflict_step_hints
string-array.item: Stick to observable events: who, what, when. Avoid words like \'always\' or \'never\'.
Try to name specific emotions — not just \'angry\' but \'humiliated\', \'ignored\', \'disrespected\'.
Try to assume positive or neutral intent. What pressures or fears might they have had?
This isn\'t about blame, it\'s about growth. Even small things count.
It could be a conversation, an apology, setting a boundary, or simply letting it go.

Discover what consistently sets off strong reactions in you.
Step into someone else\'s perspective — even someone difficult.
Learn the crucial difference and practice responding with empathy.
Most people listen to reply. Practice listening to understand.
A mindfulness technique to release tension held in your body.
One habit that can change how you respond under stress.
Feedback is a gift — when it\'s delivered well.
Go beyond listing — explore why you\'re grateful.
Think of a moment this week when you felt uncomfortable. Instead of \'bad\' or \'stressed\', what is the most precise word for what you felt?
Was it closer to anxious, overwhelmed, or dread?
Was it frustration, resentment, or disappointment?
Was it loneliness, exclusion, or rejection?
Close your eyes and scan your body from head to toe. Where do you feel tension, tightness, or ease? What might that sensation be telling you emotionally?
Tight chest or shoulders often signal stress or anxiety
Heaviness in the stomach can mean dread or guilt
Warmth in the chest often signals joy or love
Think of 3 situations that reliably make you feel angry, anxious, or hurt. What do they have in common? What value or need is being threatened?
Common triggers: feeling ignored, losing control, being criticized
Look for patterns across different people or places
Behind every trigger is usually an unmet need

Think of someone you recently had a conflict or tension with. Try to describe the situation entirely from their point of view — their fears, pressures, and intentions. What might they have been feeling?
Assume positive or neutral intent first
What challenges might they be dealing with that you don\'t see?
How would you feel if you were in their exact situation?
Your friend says: \'I\'ve been so anxious about work lately, I can barely sleep.\' How do you respond?
\"At least you still have a job! Things could be worse.\"
This minimizes their feeling. Comparing to worse situations rarely helps — it signals that their pain isn\'t valid.
\"Oh no, that sounds really hard. What\'s been going on?\"
This is empathy — you acknowledge the feeling and invite them to share more without judgment.
\"You should try meditation, it really helped me.\"
Jumping to solutions skips over the emotional need to feel heard first. Save advice for later.
In your next conversation today, try to listen without planning your response. Just absorb. Afterward, reflect: What did you notice about the other person that you might have missed before?
Notice their tone, not just their words
What emotions are underneath what they\'re saying?
What do they seem to need from this conversation?
Find a comfortable position. Close your eyes and slowly scan from head to toe — noticing tension without judgment, letting each area soften as you breathe out.
Close your eyes and take 3 slow breaths
Bring attention to the top of your head
Slowly scan down — notice tension without judging
At each area, breathe out and let it soften
Continue all the way down to your feet
Open your eyes and notice how you feel
You get a passive-aggressive email from a colleague in front of your team. Your first instinct is to fire back immediately. What do you do?
Reply immediately and set the record straight
Reacting immediately when emotional often escalates things. Your amygdala is driving — not your best self.
Take 10 seconds, breathe, then decide if a reply is even needed now
The pause interrupts the stress response. Most situations benefit from a short delay — your reply will be clearer and calmer.
Ignore it completely and say nothing
Avoidance can work short-term but unresolved tensions tend to grow. A thoughtful response later is usually better.
A teammate keeps missing deadlines. You need to address it. How do you start the conversation?
\"You\'re always late with everything. It\'s affecting the whole team.\"
Using \'always\' and leading with blame triggers defensiveness. It\'s about them as a person, not the behavior.
\"I wanted to check in — I\'ve noticed the last two deadlines were missed. Is everything okay?\"
This opens with curiosity and specific facts. It assumes something might be wrong rather than leading with blame — much more effective.
\"Just a heads up, the team is getting frustrated.\"
Indirect feedback rarely leads to change and can feel cowardly. Be specific and direct but kind.

What is one small thing today that you might normally overlook?

string-array.name: vocab_tips
string-array.item: Allow grief its time — don\'t rush it. Writing a letter to what you\'ve lost externalises the feeling and gently begins healing.
Gentle movement and soft music can ease melancholy without forcing you to \'cheer up\'. Let yourself feel it while doing something kind for your body.
Wistfulness is a soft emotion — honour it. Write down one good memory it brings up. Gratitude for what was is a form of joy.
Send one short message to someone you care about. Connection doesn\'t require a long conversation — a simple \'thinking of you\' is enough.
Find one tiny thing within your control today — even making your bed. Small acts of agency rebuild hope one step at a time.
Name what you hoped for. Acknowledging the expectation out loud or in writing helps release the disappointment attached to it.
Break the dreaded thing into the smallest possible first step and do only that. The anticipation is almost always worse than the reality.
Ask yourself: what\'s the realistic worst case? Then ask what you\'d do if that happened. Having a plan in mind reduces fear significantly.
Vulnerability is courage, not weakness. Share what you\'re feeling with one trusted person — being witnessed and accepted heals.
Write down what you believe was unfair before saying it aloud. Clear thinking leads to more effective action than reactive words.
Resentment harms you more than the other person. Ask: what do I need to let this go? A conversation, an apology, or simply a decision to release it.
Take 10 minutes before responding to anything. Outrage narrows thinking — space lets you act with intention rather than react with emotion.
Step away for 5 minutes. A short break resets your patience and gives you perspective on what truly matters versus what just feels urgent.
Contempt creates distance. Ask whether there\'s a hurt or unmet need underneath it — addressing that is more useful than the contempt itself.
Revulsion often signals a values violation. Use it as information: what boundary was crossed, and what do you need to feel safe again?
Ask: will this delay matter in one year? If not, use this moment to practise presence. Three slow breaths can transform waiting into rest.
Bitterness is old pain with nowhere to go. Journalling about the original hurt — not the person — can begin to dissolve it over time.
